VERDICT: ACCEPTThe mathematical extension is sound, including the non-reuse theorem, the excess-loss identity, the residual-charge-five threshold, the complete resource-level first-failure classification, and the physical reservation-monotonicity counterexample. The universal grid bound is correctly left open.There is one wording clarification I recommend: the sentence that the guard  $(1,4)$  has “all its neighbors” as endpoints must mean all occupied graph neighbors. Its fourth lattice neighbor,  $(2,4)$ , is deliberately blank. Under the occupied-neighbor convention used by the degree-three freezing argument, the donor is valid; under a literal all-four-lattice-neighbors reading, that sentence would be false and the donor claim would require revision.1. Componentwise mixing and non-reuseThe mixed score
$$F(r)=\sum_C\max(K_C,W_C)$$
is valid for the stated family of rules.For each residual incidence component  $C$ , the physical slots belonging to  $C$  are disjoint from the slots in every other component. The chosen  $K_C$ -rule or  $W_C$ -rule uses distinct slots within  $C$ . Therefore, taking the union over components cannot reuse a physical unit.The half-capacity Hall proof is also correct. If  $Y$  is a subset of request copies and  $A$  is the set of runs supporting those copies, then
$$|Y|
\le \sum_{s\in A}\left\lfloor \frac{\deg(s)}2\right\rfloor
\le \frac12\sum_{s\in A}\deg(s)
\le |N(Y)|.$$
The final inequality is exactly where the incidence structure matters: each physical slot has at most two endpoints in  $A$ . This handles arbitrary partial subsets of request copies, rather than only whole groups belonging to a run. Hence Hall gives a matching to distinct actual slots.The  $K_C$ -branch is accepted under the stipulated exact incidence-rank dependency. Thus the componentwise maximum is attained, and
$$\max\left(\sum_C K_C,\sum_C W_C\right)
\le F(r)\le R$$
is correct. The note also correctly limits the exactness claim to the family that chooses one complete rule per component; it does not claim that  $F$  is the unrestricted optimum over every possible request pattern.The strict-mixture example is consistent: one component has  $(v,e,o)=(3,4,0)$ , giving  $K=3,W=4$ , and the other has  $(v,e,o)=(2,1,2)$ , giving  $K=1,W=0$ . Thus the componentwise score is  $4+1=5$ , while both global rule totals are  $4$ .2. Excess-loss identityFor one component,
$$K_C=\min(v_C,e_C),\qquad
W_C=e_C-\frac{o_C}{2}.$$
Therefore
$$e_C-\max(K_C,W_C)
=
\min\!\left(\max(0,e_C-v_C),\frac{o_C}{2}\right).$$
Summing gives the stated identity
$$E_{\mathrm{mix}}(r)
=
R-F(r)
=
\sum_C
\min\!\left(\max(0,e_C-v_C),\frac{o_C}{2}\right).$$
The interpretation is exact:if  $e_C\le v_C$ , the  $K_C$ -rule already uses every slot;if  $e_C>v_C$  but all degrees are even, then  $W_C=e_C$ ;a positive loss occurs exactly when both  $e_C>v_C$  and  $o_C>0$ .The observations about trees, unicyclic components, and all-even components follow immediately.3. Residual-charge-five thresholdThe threshold argument is correct.A positive-loss component must satisfy  $e>v$  and  $o>0$ . Components with  $v=1$  or  $v=2$  cannot lose capacity. For  $v=3$ , the only possible  $e>v$  case is  $e=4$ , consisting of two doubled edges in a  $1$ -by- $2$  bipartition; its degrees are  $4,2,2$ , hence all even. Thus no positive-loss component has  $v\le3$ .Consequently, every positive-loss component has  $v\ge4$ , and because  $K_C=v_C$  whenever  $e_C>v_C$ , it contributes at least four mixed credits. If
$$F(r)<q\le R,$$
then a positive-loss component exists, so  $F(r)\ge4$ , and the integral inequality  $F<q$  forces
$$q\ge5.$$
This correctly removes the former charge-four obstruction for the mixed certificate.4. Complete  $q=5$  first-failure classificationThe  $q=5$  classification is complete at the resource-graph level.Since  $F<5$ , one positive-loss component contributes exactly four credits and no other component can have positive capacity. Hence
$$v=4,\qquad F=4,\qquad e=R.$$
Because  $q=5\le R$ ,  $e\ge5$ . Also  $W=e-o/2\le4$  and  $o\le4$ , so  $e\le6$ . Thus
$$e=5\ \text{or}\ 6,\qquad
\sigma=R-q=e-5\in\{0,1\}.$$
For  $e=5$ , the possible bipartition sizes are  $1+3$  or  $2+2$ :the  $1+3$  case is the star with multiplicities  $(2,2,1)$ ;the  $2+2$  case has, up to row/column permutations and transposition, exactly
$$\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.$$
The first two are the two distinct weighted paths, and the last is a four-cycle with one doubled edge. In every case  $o=2$  and  $W=4$ .For  $e=6$ ,  $W\le4$  forces  $o=4$ . A  $1+3$  bipartition has a degree-six central vertex and therefore cannot have all four degrees odd. The only possibility is  $2+2$ , with every row and column sum equal to three. The unique matrix up to the stated symmetries is
$$\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}.$$
So the first-failure classification is complete for the residual resource graphs. The note correctly does not claim that every one of these shapes has a frozen physical realization.5. Manual audit of the frozen donor witnessThe  $8\times8$  witness is physically consistent without relying on the checker output.The ten displayed matching edges are pairwise disjoint, all are cardinal-adjacent, and they cover exactly the twenty  $P$ -vertices. They are disjoint from the twelve selected  $T$ -vertices.The  $2\times2$  blocks containing  $P$ -vertices are exactly nine receiver tiles, and those blocks contain nine selected vertices in total. The endpoint-free blocks are
$$Q_{11},Q_{12},Q_{21},Q_{22},Q_{30},Q_{31},Q_{32},$$
with capacities
$$1,1,2,1,2,2,2,$$
so
$$D=11.$$
Their residual incidence matrix, with horizontal runs as rows and vertical runs as columns, is
$$A=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&1&1\\
0&2&1\\
2&2&2
\end{pmatrix}.$$
It is connected and has
$$e=11,\qquad v=6,$$
with horizontal degrees  $2,3,6$  and vertical degrees  $2,5,4$ . Exactly two run vertices have odd degree, so
$$K=\min(6,11)=6,\qquad
W=11-\frac22=10,$$
and therefore
$$F=10.$$
The donor tile is  $Q_{12}$ . It contains the selected vertex  $(3,5)$ , whose anchor is the matching endpoint  $(3,6)$ . Its opposite corner  $(2,4)$  is blank, and the guard is  $(1,4)$ .The ownership condition can be checked directly. The guard and anchor lie in the same occupied endpoint component through
$$(1,4)\;-\;(1,5)\;-\;(1,6)\;-\;(2,6)\;-\;(3,6),$$
where the links are matching or cardinal endpoint links as appropriate.The guard  $(1,4)$  has occupied neighbors
$$(0,4),\quad (1,3),\quad (1,5),$$
all of which are  $P$ -endpoints. Its remaining lattice neighbor  $(2,4)$  is the blank donor corner. Thus its occupied degree is three.The twenty ordered triples enumerate the twenty  $P$ -endpoints exactly once. In each triple, the two displayed guards are cardinal-adjacent occupied vertices. The ordering is valid under the retained-mate freezing rule: whenever a guard is a  $P$ -endpoint, its matching mate appears as a first-coordinate endpoint at an earlier stage;  $T$ -guards are immutable. Hence the induction/earliest-promotion argument excludes a mixed simultaneous promotion bundle. The witness therefore supports a fully frozen configuration.6. Exact failure of reservation monotonicityReserving the sole unit in  $Q_{12}$  deletes one edge from the resource matrix:
$$A'=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&1&0\\
0&2&1\\
2&2&2
\end{pmatrix}.$$
The graph remains connected. The degrees become
$$(1,3,6)\quad\text{and}\quad(2,5,3),$$
so  $e'=10$  and  $o'=4$ . Therefore
$$K'=6,\qquad
W'=10-\frac42=8,\qquad
F'=8.$$
The reservation count increases from  $B=0$  to  $B'=1$ , but
$$B+F=10,\qquad B'+F'=1+8=9.$$
Thus the mixed score is genuinely non-monotone under an additional owned reservation. The mechanism is exactly the claimed parity effect: one deleted slot lowers  $e$  by one but changes two even run degrees to odd, lowering  $W$  by two.This does not contradict the pure-rank monotonicity, since
$$B+K: 6\longmapsto 1+6=7.$$
It also does not contradict the target inequality. From the displayed counts,
$$|T|+|M|=12+10=22<32=\frac{8\cdot8}{2}.$$
The global slack is
$$\sigma=32-22=10.$$
Since  $D=11$ , the corrected receiver charge is  $\rho=1$ , so before reservation  $q=\rho-B=1$ , and after reservation  $q=0$ . The certificate remains sufficient in both states even though  $B+F$  decreases.7. ScopeThe note does not prove an unrestricted grid coverage inequality, a universal five-sixths bound, or a universal grid triple equality. It proves a componentwise certificate and gives an exact resource-level loss formula, then uses the frozen witness only to refute reservation monotonicity of that certificate. That scope is correctly stated.The only wording change I recommend is:Replace “all its neighbors are endpoints” by “all its occupied neighbors are endpoints.”With that convention made explicit, the note is mathematically acceptable.
